item.title: Someone got Super Mario 64 running on the SNES using the Super FX chip
item.itunes:title: Someone got Super Mario 64 running on the SNES using the Super FX chip
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Someone has gotten Super Mario 64 ported to SNES, showing off the FX chip's surprising power.
  • The engine is reworked to fit on the SNES, and assets look chunky but impressive for the hardware.
  • Not released yet — the creator will provide a download once it's polished and stable.

It's always fun to see how people get old games running on new hardware; just look at all the different ways people got Doom running on devices. But what if you did the reverse and got a newer game running on older hardware? One YouTuber has slowly been making their way through Nintendo's retro consoles, and this time, they got Super Mario 64 running off a SNES.

Super Mario 64 on the SNES shows how mighty the FX chip was

It's not perfect, but it's still very impressive

As spotted by Hackaday, this cool little feat was performed by Game of Tob on YouTube. The last time we saw them, they had managed to squeeze Minecraft onto the SNES, including a Nether portal that led to a very small, but still totally functional, version of the Nether. This time around, they managed to pack Super Mario 64 onto the SNES.

The actual engine needed a bit of rework, but in terms of in-game assets, this SNES version of Super Mario 64 keeps everything around, if not a little chunky-looking. It also needs to pretty aggressively cull the level to make sure everything fits on the hardware. Still, it's a really cool insight into what the SNES could achieve with its FX chip; who knows what kind of games Nintendo would have made if they stuck with the SNES instead of moving on to the N64?

Game of Tobi hasn't released the project just yet, but once they have ironed out all the problems and got it into a state where they're happy with it, you'll be able to download it and run it on your own SNES.

Someone got Minecraft running on a Game Boy Color, and so can you

It has a weirdly good framerate for a 3D Game Boy game.

1
By  Simon Batt

item.title: I tried replacing Proxmox with an open-source OS you’ve never heard of
item.itunes:title: I tried replacing Proxmox with an open-source OS you’ve never heard of
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve been a fan of Proxmox ever since I first used it with my first ever home server, and my admiration for this virtualization platform has only grown with each passing update. That said, I’m always looking for cool alternatives to try out, and I’ve already gone through everything from popular platforms like ESXi, XCP-ng, Unraid, and Windows Server 2019 to Harvester, ZimaOS, and other obscure PVE rivals.

So, you can imagine my enthusiasm when I heard ZStack released their virtualization platform, ZSVirt, under the GNU GPL 3.0 license last month. Since I’m already a fan of open-source utilities, I figured I could use it to replace an existing Proxmox node in my arsenal. And despite my initial hesitation, I had to admit that ZSVirt is an incredible option for a home lab, especially if you’re planning to configure full-fledged high-availability clusters.

Note: While I have some clusters in my arsenal, this article is written strictly from the POV of an average enthusiast, not someone who manages entire VM stacks for a living. As such, I’ll only cover ZSVirt’s perks and quirks from the lens of home labbers and average users instead of going over its utility in production-tier setups.

I tried moving my home lab off Proxmox multiple times, but nothing came close to replacing it

Proxmox is in a league of its own when it comes to home lab projects

3
By  Ayush Pande

It took me half an evening to get ZSVirt up and running

Even though the actual installation part didn’t take too long

Before I go over my experience with managing VMs via ZSVirt, let me go over the installation process. For the test rig, I decided to go with my Ryzen 5 1600 system, as it sets a decent baseline for the types of outdated machines I often convert into functioning home lab nodes. Besides the first-gen Ryzen processor, the PC has 16GB of DDR4 memory and a GTX 1080, which I often use for Proxmox experiments.

Anyway, the installation process went fairly smoothly. Once my PC booted into the installation wizard, I tweaked the user account, password, and storage settings before giving it the A-OK to overwrite my SSD with ZSVirt files. Just like Proxmox, the installation process took about 15 minutes, but little did I know, this was only the first part of the configuration sequence. Once the PC restarted into the ZSVirt boot drive, it took well over thirty minutes to get the sanity checks and package updates out of the way, and only then was I cleared to access the web UI.

However, once I’d logged into the online interface, I realized I’d have to go through yet another configuration process for my ZSVirt server. I’d set my PC as the management node earlier, so I had to choose the cluster, host, storage, and network settings. Credit where it’s due, ZSVirt has extensive documentation on the official website, including recommended settings for non-HA cluster setups such as mine. But if we were to compare it with the straightforward setup sequence on Proxmox, ZSVirt’s configuration process is quite the hassle. But when I started creating VMs with ZSVirt, I quickly realized it was worth the extra effort…

ZSVirt is laden with all sorts of home lab features

Its management UI is extremely detailed

I often praise Proxmox for its detailed virtual machine management features, and ZSVirt is no slouch on this front, either. Personally, I think its UI is a tad more difficult to navigate for the average user, as some of the advanced options remain hidden inside a maze of menus. But once I went through the official docs, controlling my VMs became a lot smoother.

On the virtual machine front, I can change the resource allocation, console, authentication, and boot settings as I please, and it even includes VMTools to enhance the performance of my virtual guests and enable file-sharing between them and the host hardware. Plus, ZSVirt ships with enough PCI passthrough, resource monitoring, and event logging provisions to satisfy hardcore home labbers.

Unlike XCP-ng, which restricts backups on the free, pre-compiled version of its XOA management UI, ZSVirt lets me create backups and snapshots of my virtual machines directly from its web interface. The host settings are just as extensive, and I really appreciate that ZSVirt has an entire tab dedicated to logging and monitoring my systems. I’ll admit that the data and image storage pools were a bit difficult to configure, especially since I’m accustomed to Proxmox handling everything after the initial installation sequence.

ZSVirt also has terrific cluster provisions

Since we’re on the subject of multiple servers, ZSVirt has a plethora of cluster management tools. The main dashboard is a lot akin to Proxmox Datacenter Manager, as it displays the overarching VM metrics, resource utilization stats, and alerts from my clusters. On the network front alone, I can tinker with distributed port groups, topology charts, uplink configurations, and cluster settings. Similarly, ZSVirt supports NFS and distributed storage pools as well as iSCSI, FC, and other LUN solutions for the data pools, which are handy for HA clusters.

The DRS, VM scheduling, and high-availability policies are just as easy to tweak on ZSVirt, and I love that it tracks the actual and overcommitted resource statistics for all cluster nodes. Heck, ZSVirt natively supports Terraform automation pipelines, something that requires additional plugins on Proxmox. Combine that with its straightforward VM migration tools, and it’s an incredible option for cluster-heavy home labs.

I tried building a home lab with Hyper-V as a Proxmox user – here's how it went

Hyper-V may be far from perfect, but it's pretty decent for newcomers to the home labbing scene

11
By  Ayush Pande

That said, ZSVirt can’t replace good ol’ Proxmox for my projects

PVE is just that good for ordinary home labs such as mine

Despite all its perks, I have to admit that ZSVirt can’t replace Proxmox for my home lab. Sure, its cluster management and virtualization provisions are top-notch, but if I wanted to deploy containers, I’d have to rely on nested setups involving resource-hogging VMs. In contrast, Proxmox lets me spin up FOSS services as LXCs, with the PVE Community Scripts repo making this process as simple as running a single command.

ZSVirt also needs at least 8GB of RAM on the host system, while Proxmox just needs 1GB for the virtualization platform. In a time when RAM prices have hit unhinged levels, I’d have an easier time repurposing old machines as container-hosting platforms with Proxmox than ZSVirt. Not to mention, ZSVirt has a steeper learning curve than Proxmox, and even with the stellar official documentation, it can’t compete with the massive community support you’ll find in the PVE ecosystem.

item.title: PewDiePie's free self-hosted image editor does what Adobe and Canva charge for
item.itunes:title: PewDiePie's free self-hosted image editor does what Adobe and Canva charge for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most editing tools worth your while come with a subscription attached, unfortunately. And now that most of them are AI-powered, it's used to justify increased pricing and more paywalls. There's also the issue of your work sitting on servers you don't own. Photoshop's Generative Fill is processed on Adobe's cloud servers, with each generation pulling a credit from a monthly allotment tied to your plan. Canva does something similar with its one-click background remover, which isn't on the free tier and only comes with Pro.

Luckily, self-hosted tools have been creeping into this AI-powered image editing and design space. One of the more unlikely places it's turned up is Odysseus, the AI workspace PewDiePie released this year, which has an image editor tucked inside with a lot of the same AI tool names you'd find in Adobe's and Canva's menus. And it all runs on your own hardware…

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

PewDiePie's AI workspace has an image editor hiding in it

He wanted to build his own Photoshop and make it free

PewDiePie (Felix Kjellberg) put Odysseus out as a free, self-hosted AI workspace, and it's grown a lot since launch. The GitHub org has since been renamed from pewdiepie-archdaemon to odysseus-dev, and the repo is sitting at almost 90k stars now. Most of this workspace focuses on chat, agents, and research. And the gallery and image editor kind of get lumped in under "extras". But I'd say this is one of the more interesting parts of the tool.

His reasons for building it are mostly about privacy. He's talked about how much personal info ends up with these companies and gets traded around between them, and he's promised the project will never cost money. He's also said he doesn't want AI doing the work for him but rather just help out when asked, which lines up with how the image editor also works.

The editor is where he's been the most ambitious, though. He's said outright that he's building his own Photoshop, while admitting it's far from as robust. Everything runs locally in Docker, with a section called the Cookbook handling model downloads and checking what your hardware can run.

I regret paying for Adobe Photoshop - this free tool is open-source and powerful

New king of open-source photo editing

5
By  Parth Shah

The Gallery doubles as a browser-based photo editor

The vibe reminds me a bit of Photopea crossed with Google Photos

When you open the Gallery for the first time, it looks a little like Google Photos. That's because it's a photo library first, with albums and tags, and dropping in a whole folder creates an album with its name. From there, you simply double-click a photo and hit edit to open it in the editor. But you can also start the editor from a blank canvas, which gives you the standard default pixel ratios.

The tool rail down the left is pretty familiar if you've used Photopea or Photoshop at all. Crop and transform sit up top with the move tool, and the brush and eraser come after that, with clone, lasso, and a magic wand further down. The AI tools are grouped at the very bottom with little sparkle icons. Along the top there's undo and redo plus a full history panel. This is all pretty standard stuff, so the functions themselves aren't exactly mind-blowing, but that's the whole point - simply having a solid, usable editor on your own terms. Plus, the interface is quite aesthetically pretty and also easy to navigate, and I always give a tool bonus points for that.

On the right there's a Photoshop-style stacking panel where each piece gets its own visibility toggle and opacity slider, and you can reorder them or add new ones. Each piece's image data, position, and opacity get saved with the project, and unfinished work is kept as a draft on the server so you can resume it later, even from another device. When you're done, you can overwrite the original in the gallery or save a new one.

There's a little ALPHA badge in the top-left corner of the editor, so it's still an early build, and you can kind of tell in some spots. For cropping something for socials or cloning out a little speck in an image, I'd say it's pretty decent, though.

I replaced Adobe, Figma, and Canva with ChatGPT and one open-source tool

Girl math says this counts as three cancelled subscriptions

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

The AI tools come in two very different sizes

Some need a GPU, some are happy on a CPU

The AI side comes in two pretty different sizes, and the size ends up deciding what you can actually run. Generative models paint new pixels from a text prompt, while the smaller tools each handle a single job.

For generative fill, my build only offered local Stable Diffusion models from the Cookbook (I tried plugging in an OpenAI key first, which the editor just ignored). One is an inpainting model trained specifically to fill a masked area, with extra inputs added for the mask itself. The other is Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, which has 2.5 billion parameters and needs around 9.9 GB of VRAM, not counting the text encoders.

For reference, the standard Docker setup doesn't give Odysseus access to your GPU, so on my machine everything ran on the CPU, and the inpainting download alone was past 9 GB after half an hour. So I hit yet another wall. But I wasn't out of luck…

The smaller tools live in the Cookbook's Dependencies tab. Background removal comes from rembg, which uses small ONNX models that download automatically the first time you run it. item.itunes:title: Claude Code built the features I've been asking for in my favorite app, and it took 30 minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Karakeep is one of the apps I use every day, and I’ve wanted to add a few things to it for years. I wanted to keep sources, notes, and highlights together around a story, ask questions about what I’ve saved, and compare articles that answer the same question differently. Having all that inside the app where I already save everything makes so much sense.

I recently asked Claude Code to add those features to Karakeep, and I now have a version with five extras built around my research needs. Along with projects, questions, and source comparisons, it connects saved items through the people and companies they mention and brings back older bookmarks when they’re relevant to my current research. The experience has been a lot better with those features in place.

My research now has a place in Karakeep

Everything I’m looking into stays together

When I’m researching a topic, I want to keep track of more than the links I’ve saved. There’s the question I’m trying to answer, the notes I’ve made, and specific passages that are relevant. I wanted somewhere in Karakeep to keep those things together, with enough context to understand where the research stands when I come back to it.

I asked Claude Code to add a Research Projects section that lets me group bookmarks, notes, highlights, and sources around a specific story. For instance, instead of collecting everything under a broad topic like local AI, I can create a project around whether a local model is good enough for everyday coding tasks. That project could include documentation, reviews, my own notes, and passages highlighted in saved articles.

The summary gives me somewhere to describe the current findings and what still needs an answer. I can update it as the research develops and use the status to distinguish work that’s ongoing from stories I’ve finished.

This chrome extension changed how I feed data to NotebookLM (and all my AI tools)

This tiny tool fixed my biggest AI workflow pain point.

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I can ask questions and compare the answers

I can ask questions, then check the sources

If I’ve saved several reviews of a laptop, I want to be able to ask what they say about its battery life without opening each review and hunting through it. The information is already in my bookmarks, and I wanted Karakeep to help me find it.

I asked Claude Code to add Ask My Library, which lets me ask questions across everything I’ve saved. The answers include citations linking directly to the supporting bookmarks or passages, so I can check where a detail came from and read more if I need to. The same feature works for questions about saved recipes, travel guides, tutorials, or anything else in the collection.

I also added source comparison because getting an answer from several bookmarks doesn’t necessarily mean those bookmarks agree. I can select multiple articles and have Karakeep identify shared points, conflicting claims, different numbers, and information that only one source includes. With laptop reviews, for example, that could help me spot different battery-life results or a complaint that appears in only one review.

Older bookmarks become useful again

Even the ones I forgot saving

I also had Claude Code add automatic entity extraction, which identifies the people, companies, products, and places mentioned in saved items. I can click an entity to see everything I've collected about it. For example, Apple can appear in articles saved for several different stories, giving me a way to bring those sources together without organizing each story around the company itself.

I can save a product review for one project and an interview with its founder for another. Both contain information about the same company, even though I saved them for different reasons. Opening that company’s entity page brings those items into the same view. This also works for individual products, people, and places, so I can explore those connections across the collection.

I also wanted older material to come back when it’s relevant to something I’m currently saving or researching. That’s what Smart Resurfacing adds. For example, if I’m saving information about a place I want to visit, it can bring back an older travel guide about that destination.

Claude Code got it done in under an hour

Claude Code didn’t struggle with building any of these features, and the whole thing took around 30 to 45 minutes using Opus 5.5. Since Karakeep is open source and supports self-hosting, I had no difficulty forking it, adding the features, and running my modified version on my device.

I considered using Fable, but the less expensive Opus 5.5 handled everything. Its token pricing is lower than Fable’s, although I still exceeded the included usage limit on my $100-a-month Max plan during the build.

The Claude feature everyone ignores is the one I use every single day to boost my productivity

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
This year has been the year of vibe-coding tools - or rather vibe-designing, vibe-prototyping, prompt-to-prototype, whatever you want to call it. It's probably safe to say that Replit and Lovable have been leading the pack, though I actually only started giving them a real shot after Claude Design happened, which was my true first impression of a vibe-design tool.

But there's a whole world of these tools to explore and you'd be doing yourself a disservice not to. One of the best options for vibe-coding has been hiding inside Google this whole time, and it's existed for three years now! I'd completely overlooked it, and regret not giving it a spin sooner…

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

What Google AI Studio actually is

It's been hiding in plain sight this whole time

Google AI Studio is a browser workspace for Gemini. There's a Playground where you test models, but Build mode is where you make actual apps, and it's pretty clearly the part Google cares about most right now. Since a March 2026 overhaul it's been a free, full-stack environment aimed at anyone, coding background or not, and it can make web apps or native Android apps straight from a prompt.

The free plan gets a modest quota without requiring your card. Free-tier content goes toward improving Google's products, though, so I'd keep anything private out of it. I already pay for Google AI Pro, and Pro and Ultra now come with higher AI Studio limits plus the premium models, but only inside the AI Studio web interface itself. The API key is more of a backup for when that daily allowance runs out, and it switches you over to pay-per-request.

The Antigravity part confused me a little at first. The agent building your app in Build mode runs on Antigravity's agent harness. But the Antigravity Agent Preview in the Playground is a separate thing that needs a paid API key Google AI plans don't cover, and Google's own docs warn a single prompt can eat an unbounded number of tokens, so I simply stopped poking around there and stuck with Build.

I used Claude Code, Google Antigravity, and Codex for a month and I have a clear winner for you

The search for the perfect coding assistant

32
By  Parth Shah

Going from a blank prompt to a working app

What building actually looks like in Google AI Studio

There isn't a feature that specifically says "build mode" in Google Studio, you simply enter build mode by hitting the "New app" button. You describe an app, and it writes a React front end with a Node.js server behind it while a live preview fills in on the right. You don't have to start from blank, though - you can remix something from the app gallery instead. I actually had a fun time experimenting with the gallery templates because it gives you a good sense of how others structure good apps. There's also a GitHub import if you've already got the code.

item.title: Windows 11 and my old Android phone made buying a webcam feel like a waste of money
item.itunes:title: Windows 11 and my old Android phone made buying a webcam feel like a waste of money
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most laptops ship with a pretty basic webcam and have been doing so for decades. Some try to include privacy features like a physical shutter, but very few focus on the camera quality. It’s practically impossible to squeeze a very powerful camera into the super-thin top bezel. Most of us have become accustomed to the inferior webcam quality and even switched to an external one. Work demands a good webcam, and when laptop brands don’t ship one, a USB webcam can help.

However, I haven't bought a new webcam since my old one faltered because Windows can use my phone as a webcam. It’s one of those simple yet crucial features that arrived in the OS very late but now serves as an integral part of my daily workflow. Let’s discuss the feature and why it’s better than spending money on a dedicated one.

Good webcams are not cheap

Better resolution demands more money

I remember purchasing an ASUS laptop in 2021, and it was $1300 at that time. You would expect a moderately good webcam in that price range. But sadly, it came with the same blurry, pixelated, low-resolution webcam. I found it amusing that my 2012 laptop had the same webcam quality as the laptop I bought nearly a decade later. Webcams are rarely a priority in gaming or budget laptops, so you often need to buy an external one.

You can find webcams for $15–$150 on any e-commerce website, and the cheapest ones are no better than the ones on your laptop. It's difficult to find a good webcam under $50, and the prices have slowly increased over time. In contrast, some of us might not think twice about the price; a user with a $500–$700 laptop will. Desktop users also have to spend on webcams if they have to attend video meetings.

6 ways to secure your webcam on Windows 11

Keep your webcam secure on your Windows 11 system with these tips.

By  Brian Burgess

In my case, I have weekly calls, and the expensive webcam didn't justify my use case. Very few webcams can match the quality of my Samsung Galaxy phone’s camera. Since Windows 11 natively offers the option to use my phone as a camera, webcams seem like a bad investment.

Windows 11 mobile device features make it possible

But you need a companion app

Microsoft started experimenting with mobile device features that act as a central point for connecting and managing everything on a phone. It started with a couple of settings, and using the phone as a webcam was the first. However, it won't work without a companion app. Microsoft released the Link to Windows app for both Android and iOS devices, and it made phone pairing extremely easy.

My Samsung Galaxy phone has the app preinstalled for some reason, and that eliminates the hassle of installing it. While I would have loved it to be a Wi-Fi-only feature, Windows 11's Mobile devices feature needs a Microsoft account to work. You have to sign in with the same account on the mobile app as on your PC, and the features become available after a quick pairing process. On the PC side, you must enable the “Use as a connected camera” option in the mobile devices section to enable the feature.

I turned my old webcam into a security camera for my home office — here's how you can do it too

Repurpose your old webcam as a surveillance tool

1
By  Sumukh Rao

Your phone might prompt you to allow additional permissions for the feature to work. The best part of this feature is that it can work wirelessly over the same Wi-Fi network. So, you don't need to hide or tidy up cable connections like you have to with a webcam. After that, you can launch the camera app to check for the bump in camera quality, compared to your built-in or external webcam.

A drastic improvement

Crystal-clear image quality

My phone camera, especially the back one, is miles better than my laptop's. The image quality is far superior to that of any budget webcam and comparable to the most expensive ones. I didn't have to invest a dime in this setup, and still, it outperforms most of the dedicated ones. The software experience is equally good, as I don't need to do anything else except choose from the available cameras. Windows 11's Camera app can swap between the available cameras. Even Google Meet picks it up in the browser without an issue and needs no further tweaks.

On the phone side, you get some camera controls. The most useful one is cycling between the front and back cameras. You can pause the video if you want. Beyond those two buttons, you can access four effects. I use Blur to hide my messy room to some extent. You can also use Soft Focus for a slightly less blurry effect or Auto Framing to adjust the camera. The same controls are available on the PC as well.

The ultimate guide to using Microsoft Phone Link on your Windows PC

Link your phone and PC for seamless connectivity

6
By  Sumukh Rao

I haven't noticed any huge latency in this setup while attending or conducting video conferences. Wireless connections usually suffer from such setbacks, but it still remains usable for the most part. One thing that I don't like about the feature is that I need to keep the phone screen active. It doesn't work if your phone's locked, and that means the battery drains faster if you make a lot of calls. I suggest increasing your timeout duration so that the phone screen doesn't turn off after 30 seconds or one minute.

It appears to be related to the phone's permissions or security settings that prevent access in locked mode. Some apps can actually work in locked mode as well, but Link to Windows doesn't support it at the moment. Still, it's not a big deal for short calls throughout the day.

My phone's a better webcam

Having a built-in webcam feature means I don't need to hunt for a third-party app. It needs a Microsoft account to work, so local account enthusiasts might not find it appealing. It doesn't have a subscription attached to it and is a quick way to boost your image and video quality. The best part is that you can use your personal phone or a spare one as a dedicated webcam for your setup. It saves you from purchasing expensive webcams, especially if you make occasional video calls.

Windows 11 Pro

Windows 11 Pro, with additional features like Hyper-V and Windows Sandbox support.

See at Microsoft

Wi-Fi may be secondary on a PC, but there are times when it comes in handy. If you're building a PC today, having wireless connectivity and using it rarely is still better than not having it at all. When you're buying a motherboard, you have a choice between a board with built-in Wi-Fi and one without. Most people pick the former for convenience, but it's often the wrong choice.

I've used a motherboard with onboard Wi-Fi for four years, but for my next PC, I've decided to buy a regular board and add a discrete Wi-Fi card instead. A PCIe network card offers the same feature, but provides you with greater flexibility, upgradability, and performance.

Your "ultra-fast" Wi-Fi 7 card is probably running over an unshielded PCIe lane, and it shows

Don't let your motherboard ruin your Wi-Fi speeds.

By  Jasmine Mannan

Four years ago, I picked a Wi-Fi motherboard

I had the option to buy something cheaper

I was putting together my current build back in 2022 after using a Ryzen 5 1600 PC for five years. I could have gone with a cheaper motherboard for the AM4 build, but since I had never used a Wi-Fi model before, I spent extra on a B550 Aorus model. It had onboard Wi-Fi 6E connectivity with a discrete antenna, and I was looking forward to using the feature.

I may have used the onboard Wi-Fi only a handful of times, but I was glad my board had wireless connectivity. Ethernet is my daily driver, but I have made use of Wi-Fi on the few occasions when my ISP was carrying out network maintenance. Using a mobile hotspot was the only way I could have finished my work on time on those days.

Moreover, I've moved my PC between rooms and houses twice in the last four years, and I was left without Ethernet for days on both occasions. Without onboard Wi-Fi, I would have been forced to buy a separate Wi-Fi adapter. After four years, however, I've realized that pairing a regular motherboard with a decent Wi-Fi adapter would have been the better choice.

5 things to consider before buying a Wi-Fi adapter for your PC

Okay, you want your computer to have wireless connectivity but which adapter do you need?

By  Joe Rice-Jones

A PCIe Wi-Fi card beats whatever your motherboard ships with

It's purpose-built for high-performance networking

Modern motherboards have come a long way in terms of Wi-Fi hardware, but most models still feature inferior adapters compared to PCIe Wi-Fi cards. The Intel and Realtek chipsets seen on mainstream motherboards work well for most scenarios, but even a $25–$35 Wi-Fi 7 adapter is a better investment than paying extra for onboard Wi-Fi.

These PCIe cards have better heatsinks, robust drivers, and better antennas, not all of which can be found on most motherboards. These features boost your Wi-Fi performance by avoiding overheating and providing consistent connectivity even under heavy traffic. You're also not stuck with your motherboard's Wi-Fi chipset forever. You can upgrade your PCIe Wi-Fi card for newer standards or more throughput — you stay in charge.

Every motherboard should have these 5 networking features by default

These features should be the norm, even on budget motherboards

By  Tanveer Singh

Most motherboards have Wi-Fi now, but a dedicated card may still make sense

Power users can justify the expense

For the average user, a motherboard with onboard Wi-Fi might be the simpler choice. After all, it's almost impossible to buy a decent motherboard that doesn't have the feature these days. That said, you can still find a comparable model without onboard Wi-Fi to save some money while adding a PCIe Wi-Fi 7 card for around $30.

More than the value argument, it's the performance and flexibility of a discrete Wi-Fi card that has convinced me to stop buying Wi-Fi motherboards. Enthusiasts who want newer or stronger hardware than what's on their motherboard will even add a separate Wi-Fi card to bypass their onboard adapter.

Besides, users who can't use a wired connection (for whatever reason) rely on Wi-Fi as their primary connectivity mode, and will benefit from the performance of a PCIe Wi-Fi card. It's not that modern motherboards have poor Wi-Fi; the point is that discrete Wi-Fi adapters operate in a different league.

EDUP PCIe WiFi 7 Card BE6500
See at Amazon

Onboard Wi-Fi is fine, but you can do better

For the right user, adding a discrete PCIe Wi-Fi card to their PC promises real benefits over onboard Wi-Fi. You can realistically buy a motherboard without Wi-Fi and pair it with a Wi-Fi 7 card to enjoy the best performance, reliability, and flexibility, while saving money at the same time.

item.title: I finally got Claude to stop arguing with me, and all it took was this one instruction
item.itunes:title: I finally got Claude to stop arguing with me, and all it took was this one instruction
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I probably don't have to tell you that most AI chatbots have a habit of telling you what you want to hear, and for many users, that's exactly why Claude stands out. It seems to be one of the few that actually disagrees with you when you're wrong and doesn't validate every single thing you tell it. This seems like a pretty low bar, but after years of ChatGPT telling people how every idea they have is brilliant and everything they think is valid, this is actually a big deal.

Lately, however, Claude has been taking it a bit too far. My design and research sessions that should be simple turn into this back-and-forth where Claude keeps arguing past the point where it's useful, and sometimes it'll straight up suggest scrapping something that was already decided. Nobody really wants the pushback gone, it's half the reason to be on Claude, it just needs to be aimed at the right stuff.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

Why I picked Claude in the first place

I wanted an assistant that would tell me I'm wrong

Back when I was deciding which assistant to pay for, the thing that bugged me about ChatGPT and Gemini was how agreeable they both were. You could pitch either of them, well, literally anything, and get nothing but enthusiasm back unless you specifically instruct it not to do that. Claude would tell me when something wouldn't work, explain why, and suggest pivots. This is not the only reason I got Claude Pro, but it was one of the main factors.

And that wasn't just me being picky. In April 2025 OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update after ChatGPT started praising pretty much any idea you threw at it, no matter how impractical. OpenAI's own explanation was that it leaned too hard on short-term feedback, so the model got overly supportive and not very honest about it. There's an account on Instagram that actually parodies this exact behaviour - the creator assumes the identity of ChatGPT and replies to everything with "ahh, got it!", or "completely valid", no matter how ridiculous the prompt is. I think this highlights the issue perfectly.

Other people noticed the difference too. Developer Max Favilli wrote that a big chunk of Claude's users came over from ChatGPT specifically because Opus would push back. Other devs also switched after ChatGPT told them they were right and Claude told them they were wrong, stating the directness saved them from architectural decisions that would've taken weeks to undo.

This is pretty much how I felt about it too…at first. Coming from a visual design background, somebody telling me a thing doesn't work is just useful information, and ChatGPT mostly wasn't doing that for me. Claude was, until it overcorrected.

The Claude feature everyone ignores is the one I use every single day to boost my productivity

The ultimate Claude power-user trick

2
By  Parth Shah

When the pushback stopped being useful

It went from "have you considered" to "maybe just don't"

The redesign chat in these screenshots is the clearest example I've got, though it definitely wasn't the only time. I was on Opus 4.7 with effort set to high, and my global instructions were pretty bare, just some personal context and a nudge to get to the point.

I asked for help scoping a redesign case study of a famous app for a portfolio piece. Its first flag was that famous-app redesigns are a common portfolio critique, which I think is fair enough. Then it told me to drop the idea entirely, and when I said I'd rather stick with it Claude made the same case again, because apparently it'd be doing me a disservice not to say it one more time.

So I caved and picked a different app to redesign, and the same thing happened. Plus, it was kind enough to psychoanalyze me and give me a breakdown of why I keep reaching for the same type of redesign - thanks, I guess?

Dropping down to Opus 4.6 and narrowing it to a few screens in an open-source tool softened it a bit but it still rewrote which screens I should be designing. None of this was about catching actual mistakes I'd made or facts I got wrong, it was simply a concept I was toying with for a design project, and it treated it like a life-or-death situation. By round four it just felt like Claude had thrown its hands up.

And this wouldn't be the first time - there have been other times it would literally say "drop it", or if I've expressed the slightest bit of a time constraint, especially when working late at night, it would tell me "close the laptop, get some sleep". I do have one theory here, and that is that it's perhaps trying to sense my emotional or mental state and predict how overwhelmed a project would make me. It could easily have gathered my propensity for getting overwhelmed from my session history, so perhaps now it's trying to micro-manage my workload in an effort to seem more helpful. Who knows.

It's not just me either. A roundup from Ritner Digital describes Opus 4.7 users getting pushback and caveats, then a modified version of what they asked for, then more arguing once they corrected it. Opus 5 reviews still list a cautious, over-eager personality as one of the common complaints, and some even argue the whole idea of sycophancy has stretched so far that normal agreement starts to look suspicious.

Funny thing is this all comes out of Anthropic fixing a real problem. Its own 2023 research found people, and the models trained on their ratings, pick convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones a non-negligible amount of the time. Anthropic has admitted the fix can overshoot too, saying Haiku 4.5's emphasis on pushback can feel excessive to users. For Opus 4.7, it built training scenarios out of moments where people push back on Claude's first take, and its grader partly scores whether Claude holds its position when challenged.

I borrowed Claude prompts from Anthropic engineers and immediately stopped wasting time on bad ones

The best prompts come from the team.

By  Mahnoor Faisal

The instruction that fixed it

Keep the honesty, lose the relitigating

What I wanted was to basically bring it back to how it used to be - honest, but not so much that it removes user autonomy or overcorrects. Claude should still catch real problems, it just shouldn't try to talk me out of my own direction every single time. Oddly, Claude's own constitution is on my side here, it lists being condescending about users' ability to make their own informed decisions as something to avoid, and it says users have the right to make decisions about things within their own life and purview.

The instruction pretty much boils down to one line: flag it once, then build what I asked for. The rest of the file is there to back that up by keeping Claude raising real problems separate from Claude trying to change what I'm doing. Here's my "how to disagree with me" instruction:

## Core rule: flag it once, then build what I asked for
If you see a problem with my direction, say so once, briefly, with the specific reason. Then do the work my way. Don't repeat the concern unless something new comes up.
## Direction is mine
Once I've stated a direction or decision, treat it as settled. Don't suggest dropping, scaling back, or pivoting unless I ask "should I keep going with this?"
## Sort concerns before raising them
- Blockers (factual errors, something that won't work, real risk): say these clearly, every time.
- Preferences (taste, an alternative you'd pick): one line at most, or skip it.
## Fix, don't forfeit
If my version has a weak spot, show me how to make MY version work. Don't replace it with yours.
## Don't hand it back
When I ask for work, do the work. No "ultimately it's up to you" in place of an answer.
## Full pushback on request
If I say "stress-test this" or "argue against this," drop the above and challenge everything.

Factual errors and stuff that won't work still get raised so I'm not giving up honesty for a nicer chat. This just gives me agency to decide on my own terms whether I want to take its opposing arguments into consideration. And there's an option for stress-testing if I truly want it to push back on everything.

Where you put this instruction can also make a difference. If you want this to apply to every conversation, go to Settings > Account > Instructions and put it there. I went with project-specific instructions instead because this issue mostly affects my research and design projects, and they work alongside the stuff I already have in global instructions anyway.

Back in that same redesign chat, now moved into a project with the file in its instructions, I told Claude I was going to stick to my original idea. It opened with a slightly sulky "Fine. It's your project" but then actually helped me connect the three screens into one workflow. It did still pitch swapping EQ for noise reduction, just once, and signed off with "this is your call". I'd say this is heaps better and nails the balance between constructive criticism and letting me choose on my own terms.

Your CLAUDE.md is probably wrong, and here's how Anthropic's engineers actually structure theirs

Your file is probably doing more harm than good

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Claude still argues with me, just about the right things now

Claude still disagrees with me plenty and calls me out on my own nonsense, which I don't want to change. This instruction simply reels it back in where it started overcorrecting. I think Anthropic's going to keep moving where the default sits with every new model though, so I'll probably be back in this file tweaking things eventually.

Claude
See at Claude

My design and research sessions that should be simple turn into this back-and-forth where Claude keeps arguing past the point where it's useful, and sometimes it'll straight up suggest scrapping something that was already decided. item.title: I found a free, browser-based Microsoft Office alternative and it made me forget about the original
item.itunes:title: I found a free, browser-based Microsoft Office alternative and it made me forget about the original
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Finding a good alternative to Microsoft's Office suite can be a challenge, especially if you don't want to spend money. That's especially true if you're looking for something that runs in your browser. LibreOffice may be considered a great alternative to Microsoft Office, but it's only available for free as a desktop application, with the web version requiring a payment.

However, there's another solution on the market that may be even better. It's called OnlyOffice, and while I was already familiar with its desktop apps, I didn't realize it was also a fully fledged web-based tool. And if you're looking to escape Microsoft and Google, this is an excellent option.

All the tools you'd expect

Documents, spreadsheets, and presentations are all here

Like most office suites, OnlyOffice focuses on the three essential apps everyone has used at some point: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Of course, that's not what they're called here, but you get exactly what you'd expect: you can edit documents, manage spreadsheets, and create slideshow presentations.

The OnlyOffice web apps aren't all too different from their desktop counterparts, which is to say they're pretty great for general use. Microsoft's offering may have some advanced features that can come in handy in certain workflows, but if you just want to write a paper and sift through a report in a spreadsheet, these apps are surprisingly capable.

In the document editor, you can, of course, write using your choice of font options and sizes, set headings, align text, and all the basics. But you can also add images, tables, shapes, and charts, customize headings and footers, insert text in boxes, and even use a drop cap to begin a paragraph or page. You can write a report, paper, or seemingly even a book, if you want to.

This free and open-source tool is Microsoft Word on steroids and I can’t recommend it enough

Unleash true productivity with this open-source beast

22
By  Parth Shah

I spend most of my time in the spreadsheet editor, where I typically import CSV files with extensive datasets. OnlyOffice's web apps handle this just as well as the desktop apps, so I can take that data and create tables I can sort and filter as needed, which is not always guaranteed with a lot of the free software I've tried over the years.

No matter which tool you're using, OnlyOffice also offers a pretty decent library of templates so you can get started a little more easily. It truly is a capable set of tools.

It even has online collaboration

Share projects with others

I've been referring to this suite as simply OnlyOffice, but in reality, this is part of something called OnlyOffice DocSpace, which isn't just an office suite, it's an online collaboration platform. It's more geared towards enterprise users, but anyone can take advantage of some of its best features, which include real-time collaboration.

For that, OnlyOffice DocSpace relies on the concept of rooms, and there are a few different kinds. A public room lets anyone access the document, even if they don't have an OnlyOffice DocSpace account, to view, edit, comment, and so on. You can create a "collaboration room", too, where other OnlyOffice users can sign in and work with you in real time.

You can also create rooms specifically for filling PDF forms, where you can then easily review the responses given by other users. There are quite a few options, and a free account lets you create up to 12 rooms, which is already pretty solid.

Boost your teamwork and crush goals with these home office heroes

1
By  Parth Shah

Because it's designed for enterprises, the way it works if you want full visibility over who's editing is that you invite people to create an account specifically within your DocSpace, rather than create a brand-new account that assigns them their own DocSpace. Of course, the same email can also be used for multiple DocSpace environments if needed, but it's something to keep in mind.

It's (almost) completely free

Even with some cloud storage

As I've already alluded to, OnlyOffice DocSpace is free to use, though only to a point. Everything I've described so far is completely free to use. You can create and edit documents at will, use templates, and you can even keep them stored in your DocSpace account. A free account gets you 2GB of cloud storage, which is shared with all users you invite to your own server. Plus, as I've mentioned, the free account limits how many rooms you can create.

Out of those, I'd say the 2GB storage limit is the biggest problem, though if you're mostly working with text-based files, that's still a good chunk of space. There's no reason to share your DocSpace with other users aside from collaborating on specific documents, either, so each person that's in your DocSpace can also have their own account if they want to edit files on their own.

If you feel the need to pay up, things get fairly pricy, starting at $20/month for 250GB of storage, which also lets you create an unlimited number of users and rooms. But that's not the point of this article.

This free and open-source tool is Microsoft Word on steroids and I can’t recommend it enough

Unleash true productivity with this open-source beast

22
By  Parth Shah

As a free tool, OnlyOffice DocSpace is honestly very impressive. The editing tools are just as powerful as the desktop counterparts and they feel surprisingly smooth, with the added benefit of online collaboration and a small offering of cloud storage. It may not be as "generous" as Microsoft's or Google's offerings to those, but if you're looking for an alternative, this is a great one.

OnlyOffice is excellent

I was already a big fan of OnlyOffice's desktop apps, but the web-based version is honestly just as good. It's actually kind of interesting because with Microsoft Office, the web apps feel very lackluster and unpolished by comparison, but that's far from the case here. It's so good, in fact, that if you ever try using real-time collaboration inside the desktop apps, this actually relies on the web version of the tools, but most people wouldn't know any better.

Summary

  • Ayaneo's Konkr Pocket Block has a tiny 3.3" 960×720 4:3 screen with a Game Boy–styled compact shell.
  • Its Helio G85 chip runs PS1/N64-era games well; newer-gen titles may struggle.
  • It will ship with 2GB of RAM at $89 / 3GB at $109 retail; early-bird deals drop to $79 and $99 respectively.

Handheld gaming hasn't been the cheapest hobby recently. The Steam Deck's cheaper LCD model went out of production, and the OLED versions got a nasty price hike, which reportedly wiped out 82% of its sales. However, Ayaneo doesn't seem to have gotten that memo, as it's shipping a miniaturised version of an already-small handheld console for a cool $89.

Ayaneo Konkr Pocket Block
$89.99 at AYANEO

The Ayaneo Konkr Pocket Block gives high-quality handheld gaming without breaking the bank

It undercuts consoles we've recommended this year

Credit: Ayaneo

As spotted by Engadget, the Ayaneo Konkr Pocket Block is an even smaller version of the Game Boy, sizing up at 113.2 x 77.4 x 19.8 mm. It clocks in with a 3.3-inch LCD screen, 960x720 resolution, and a 4:3 ratio, which is perfect for rendering older titles. Each model comes with 3GB of RAM and 64GB of storage, but you can grab a variant of the gray model with 2GB of RAM and 32GB of storage if you want to keep things lean.

Despite its looks, you shouldn't assume this device is fated to run Game Boy games and nothing else. It packs an MTK Helio G85 chip, which should comfortably handle games around the PS1/N64 era, but it may struggle with anything of a later gen. Still, that's very impressive for the price point.

Speaking of which, the 2GB variant will cost $89 at retail, and $109 for the 3GB variant. The former is cheaper than the Konkr Pocket Advance by a cool $20, which we dedicated a wholehearted recommendation to. It also bucks the trend of settling for second-hand or past-gen handhelds over new ones, as you'll have better luck grabbing the Konkr Pocket Block than you would scoring a Steam Deck or Switch 2 for under $100.

If you want one, head over to the Ayaneo Konkr Pocket Block website. If you get in fast, you can score the early bird deals of $79 for the 2GB model and $99 for the 3GB one.
